doc.title: Rusty Dedrick interviewed by Monk Rowe, Ellenville, New York, June 23, 1998

title: Teaching at Manhattan School of Music
summary: He taught there 1970-80, led ensembles and taught history.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: That’s great. Now you had a whole other part of your career in the educational field, of course with the arranging but also with Manhattan.

Yeah, I liked that. I started there in ‘70 and left in ‘80 because I became 62 and I was eligible for Social Security and I thought oh boy, this is going to be great you know. So I left the job and then I’ve regretted it many times. It had a lot of advantages. One of them was prior to that, prior to 1970 I used to have rehearsal bands because I liked to write and I had some great players like Arnie Lawrence and on and on in my rehearsal band. And I didn’t have that need because I had my own bands to play. And that was an educational experience for me because I could write anything I want and bring it in the next day and play it. It was good.

Well I taught three or four ensembles, but I used to call it the concert jazz band was the A band sort of, then there was a B band and a couple of smaller groups, and I taught jazz history and appreciation courses and I liked it, it was good. Some of the players that came out of there are still doing great.
